additional_requirements.title: Proof-of-possession tokens
additional_requirements.text:
The use of bearer tokens is one of the most significant weaknesses in OAuth 2.0 protocol flows. When a bearer access token is stolen, it can immediately be abused to access protected resources. Token theft is also the reason that refresh tokens should only be used in combination with client authentication. 

Amendments to the core OAuth 2.0 specifications offer a *proof-of-possession* mechanism. Such a mechanism forces the client to prove possession of a secret when using an access token or refresh token. Abusing a stolen token becomes significantly harder, as the attacker would also have to steal the client's secret. 


### Proof-of-possession tokens 

In practice, proof-of-possession is typically implemented using a public/private key pair. The client generates a new key pair, which will be the secret for this particular bearer token. The bearer token is associated with the public key of the key pair. On every use, the client signs a challenge with the corresponding private key. The receiving party can now use the previously associated public key to verify the signature of the challenge. If they match, the client proved the possession of the private key.

The concept of proof-of-possession can take many forms in an OAuth 2.0 architecture. Proof-of-possession can be applied on access tokens, refresh tokens, as well as on authorization codes. Doing so irrefutably binds the token or code to a particular client. Techniques to enable proof-of-possession mechanisms are the use of *mutual TLS (mTLS)* or the use of *token binding*. 

Unfortunately, implementing proof-of-possession tokens requires a significant amount of control over the client application. AS a result, proof-of-possession tokens are mainly used in native applications, running either on a client device or on a server device. 


### Practical mechanisms to implement proof-of-possession

#### Mutual TLS

The first mechanism is the use of mutual TLS. When mutual TLS is used, the client is required to use a client certificate to initialize TLS connections to the authorization server and resource server. Such a connection only succeeds if the client uses the private key corresponding to the public key in the certificate.

In an OAuth 2.0 architecture, the authorization server can bind access tokens to a particular client certificate. When a resource server receives such a token, it will only accept it if the underlying TLS connection uses the same certificate. To use the certificate, the client will need access to the private key. As a result, a stolen access token can only be used together with the private key belonging to the certificate. 

More details are available in [this specification](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-oauth-mtls-12).


#### Token binding

The second mechanism to implement proof-of-possession is known as TLS Token Binding. Token binding is a suite of specifications related to the TLS protocol to enable the binding of tokens to a particular connection. Concretely, the specifications explain how to generate the secrets, how to negotiate the parameters, and how to enable the binding of tokens to the secret.

Within an OAuth 2.0 architecture, the TLS token binding mechanism can be used to bind a token to a particular client. The TLS token binding specification uses a client-based public/private key pair to establish a long-lived secret across multiple TLS connections. Linking this token binding secret to a token or code effectively ties it to the client. Due to the implementation of TLS token binding, the details are quite intricate, especially for access tokens and authorization codes.

More details are available in [this specification](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-oauth-token-binding-08).

additional_requirements.title: Securing client registration
additional_requirements.text:
Client registration is a cornerstone of securing OAuth 2.0 protocol flows. Without client registration, the authorization server would have no way of identifying a particular client. Lack of client registration also opens the door for impersonation attacks aiming to trick the user. 

Registering the client with the authorization server serves two purposes. First, it allows the developer to provide proper context information about the client. The developer can provide the authorization server with a display name, a logo, and a description. Second, the authorization server can assign a unique client identifier. This identifier plays a crucial role in identifying the client during the OAuth 2.0 protocol flows. Depending on the type of client, the authorization server also assigns a client secret.

### Public and confidential clients

The OAuth 2.0 specifications make a distinction between public and confidential clients. Public clients are clients that run in an untrusted context. This implies that they cannot keep the client credentials secret. A confidential client runs in a more trusted environment. 

This distinction plays a vital role during client registration. Public clients will receive a client identifier, but not a client secret. As a result, they can only participate in OAuth 2.0 flows that do not require client authentication. For example, a Client Credentials flow is not available to public clients. Confidential clients do receive a client secret, allowing them to participate in flows requiring client authentication.


### Client registration details

During registration, a set of client properties needs to be registered with the authorization server. These properties include the client type (public or confidential), as well as metadata about the client (display name, logo, description). 

The client's redirect URI is a crucial property. This redirect URI tells the authorization server up front where the client expects to receive the authorization code at the end of an OAuth 2.0 flow. To prevent interception of the authorization code, the authorization server requires the specification of at least one redirection URI during client registration. 

Unfortunately, the OAuth 2.0 specification does not enforce the registration of redirection URIs. It merely suggests to do so but leaves the decision up to the authorization server. Today, the following guidelines are considered mandatory for a secure deployment:

* All redirect URIs (except localhost) should use HTTPS
* Only use exact matching for redirect URIs. Do not use wildcards or hostnames.
* Redirect URIs cannot point to endpoints that respond with another redirect.

When the authorization server accepts the client registration, it generates a unique client identifier. The specification does not specify the contents of this identifier. This can be a canonical name, but might just as well be a random identifier.


### Client credentials

If the client being registered is a confidential client, the authorization server needs to establish a way to authenticate the client. The most common form to achieve this is using a client secret, but a key-based alternative is also available.

The most common mechanism to authenticate a confidential client is text-based credentials. During registration, the client receives a client ID and a client secret. Subsequently, the client can authenticate itself to the authorization server by providing the ID and secret. 

While convenient, the use of a client secret suffers from some drawbacks. Since both the authorization server and the client know the secret, it is considered to be a shared secret. Such a shared secret is more vulnerable to compromise on either end.

An alternative is using a public/private key pair for authentication. During registration, the client registers a public key with the authorization server. It keeps the private counterpart of that key in a secure location, such as a key vault. 

To authenticate, the client needs to prove possession of the private key that belongs to the registered public key. To do so, the client generates a JWT and signs it with its private key. The client sends that JWT to the authorization server, which can verify the signature using the client's registered public key. If the signature is correct, the client is authenticated. 

If possible, we recommend the use of key-based authentication over the use of a shared secret. More details on key-based authentication are available in [RFC 7523](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7523).
